To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
BenM structures with DNA reveal a highly conserved DNA-binding domain that interacts with DNA through a set of highly-conserved and a set of less-conserved amino acids.
the DNA-binding domain of a prototypical LysR-type regulator, BenM, contains two hydrophobic pockets and a hydrogen-bonding pocket that interact with DNA bases in the recognition sequence, T-N11-T.
BenM structures reveal the structural basis for recognition of a T-11-A sequence motif, and provide a framework for understanding protein-DNA interactions of LysR-type regulators.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural and molecular basis of the DNA recognition by LysR transcriptional regulators.
the structural basis for DNA recognition by the LysR-type regulator BenM.
understanding the structural and functional basis for the recognition by LTTRs of their DNA-recognition motifs, which are characterized by a T-N11-(A/T)-A sequence motif.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
LTTRs use a set of highly and poorly conserved interactions to recognize DNA.
the LTTRs are a large family of bacterial regulators with a highly conserved DNA-binding domain that interacts with a DNA-recognition motif that is usually symmetric and includes two thymines.
BenM uses highly conserved interactions with nucleotide bases, as well as numerous secondary interactions to bind DNA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
LTTRs recognize a T-N11-T sequence motif by a set of highly-conserved interactions between DNA and amino acid residues.
the DNA-binding domain of a prototypical LysR-type regulator, BenM, has a highly conserved set of residues that recognize the T-N11-A DNA-recognition motif.

the DNA-binding domain of LTTRs is highly conserved in terms of the overall fold, the DNA-binding motifs and the DNA-binding amino acids, but is highly variable in terms of the linker and the C-terminal helix.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the recognition of the DNA-recognition sequence by LTTRs is a highly specific process, which is based on interactions of the DNA with the conserved amino acids of the DNA-binding motif.

the LTTR family has developed a unique and highly conserved DNA-recognition motif, T-N11- A, and its complement, T-N11-T, which is recognized by the LTTRs through a set of highly-conserved residues in the recognition helix.
LTTRs have evolved a common set of amino acid side chains for DNA recognition, and that the recognition helix is highly flexible.
